title: Quadratic Equations
notes: Standard form: ax^2 + bx + c = 0, a not 0. A quadratic equation always has degree 2.
A real number alpha is a root if a.alpha^2 + b.alpha + c = 0. Roots of the equation = zeroes of the corresponding polynomial.
Any quadratic equation has at most 2 roots.
Two ways to solve: (1) Factorisation -- split middle term, write as product of two linear factors, set each to zero. (2) Quadratic Formula.
Discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac tells you the NATURE of roots without solving: D>0 -> two distinct real roots. D=0 -> two equal real roots. D<0 -> no real roots.
Word problems: translate carefully into one variable, form the quadratic, solve, then REJECT roots that don't make physical sense (negative length, negative age, etc.).

A pole is placed on the boundary of a circular park (diameter 13m) so the difference of distances from two diametrically opposite gates is 7m. Find the distances.
examples.solution: Using Pythagoras (angle in semicircle = 90 deg): (x+7)^2+x^2=13^2 leads to x^2+7x-60=0. D=289>0, roots x=5 or x=-12 (rejected). Distances: 5m and 12m.

exercises.question: Check whether the following are quadratic equations: (i) (x+1)^2=2(x-3) (ii) x^2-2x=(-2)(3-x) (iii) (x-2)(x+1)=(x-1)(x+3) (iv) (x-3)(2x+1)=x(x+5) (v) (2x-1)(x-3)=(x+5)(x-1) (vi) x^2+3x+1=(x-2)^2 (vii) (x+2)^3=2x(x^2-1) (viii) x^3-4x^2-x+1=(x-2)^3
exercises.answer: (i) Yes (ii) Yes (iii) No (iv) Yes (v) Yes (vi) No (vii) No (viii) Yes
